The Consumer Prices Index including owner occupiers’ housing costs (CPIH) rose by 3.7% in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 3.6% the previous month.

On a monthly basis, CPIH rose by 0.5% in October 2026, compared with a rise of 0.4% in October 2025.

The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose by 3.6% in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 3.5% the previous month.

On a monthly basis, CPI rose by 0.5% in October 2026, compared with a rise of 0.4% in October 2025.

Transport, particularly motor fuels, made the largest upward contribution to the monthly change in both CPIH and CPI annual rates; restaurants and hotels made the largest, partially offsetting, downward contribution.

Core CPIH (CPIH excluding energy, food, alcohol, and tobacco) rose by 3.1% in the 12 months to October 2026, little changed from September; the CPIH goods annual rate rose from 3.2% to 3.5%, while the CPIH services annual rate was 3.9%, little changed from September.

Core CPI (CPI excluding energy, food, alcohol, and tobacco) rose by 2.8% in the 12 months to October 2026, little changed from September; the CPI goods annual rate rose from 3.2% to 3.5%, while the CPI services annual rate was 3.7%, little changed from September.

The Consumer Prices Index including owner occupiers’ housing costs (CPIH) rose by 3.7% in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 3.6% the previous month (Figure 1).

On a monthly basis, CPIH rose by 0.5% in October 2026, compared with a rise of 0.4% in October 2025.

The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose by 3.6% in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 3.5% the previous month.

On a monthly basis, CPI rose by 0.5% in October 2026, compared with a rise of 0.4% in October 2025.

The main drivers of the annual inflation rate for CPIH and CPI are the same where they are common to both measures. However, the owner occupiers’ housing (OOH) costs component accounts for approximately 18% of the CPIH and is the main driver for differences between the CPIH and CPI inflation rates.

This makes CPIH our most comprehensive measure of inflation. We cover this in more detail in Section 4: Latest movements in CPIH inflation and provide a commentary on the CPI in Section 5: Latest movements in CPI inflation. We also cover both CPIH and CPI in Section 3: Notable movements in prices, though the figures reflect CPIH.

More information on the contents of each division can be found in Table 3 of our Consumer price inflation dataset.

Figure 2 shows the contributions from the 12 divisions to the change in the annual Consumer Prices Index including owner occupiers’ housing costs (CPIH) inflation rate between September and October 2026. These sum to the change in the annual rate, from 3.6% to 3.7%, between these months.

The increase in the 12-month rate between September and October 2026 reflected upward contributions from six divisions, partially offset by downward contributions from four divisions. The largest upward contribution came from transport, particularly motor fuels. The largest offsetting downward contribution came from restaurants and hotels.

Prices in the transport division rose overall by 7.5% in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 6.6% the previous month (Figure 3). On a monthly basis, prices rose by 0.8% in October 2026, compared with being little changed a year ago.

Figure 3: Motor fuel inflation rate was at its highest since July 2022

The largest upward effect contributing to the rise in the transport annual rate came from motor fuels.

The average price of petrol rose by 5.2 pence per litre between September and October 2026, compared with a rise of 0.7 pence per litre between September and October 2025. The average price stood at 174.7 pence per litre in October 2026. This is the highest price recorded since August 2022.

Diesel prices rose by 7.0 pence per litre in October 2026, compared with a rise of 1.2 pence per litre in October 2025. The average price stood at 199.5 pence per litre in October 2026. This is the highest price recorded since our records began in January 1996.

These movements resulted in overall motor fuel prices rising by 33.2% in the 12 months to October 2026, compared with a rise of 29.8% the previous month. This is the largest annual rise since July 2022.

Within transport, there were smaller upward effects from roadside recovery and rail, and a partially offsetting downward effect from the purchase of vehicles.

Air fares rose by 1.8% between September and October 2026, compared with a rise of 1.7% between September and October 2025. While there was an upward effect from long-haul flights, there was a counteracting downward effect from European flights.

Prices in the alcohol and tobacco division rose by 4.5% in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 2.5% in the 12 months to September. On a monthly basis, prices rose by 2.2% in October 2026, compared with a rise of 0.3% a year ago.

The rise in the 12-month rate reflected an upward effect from tobacco, where prices rose by 5.2% between September and October 2026, compared with a fall of 0.1% a year ago. The rise was possibly influenced by the timing of an increase in tobacco duty, which took effect on 1 October 2026. Duty rates on tobacco did not increase in 2025 until 26 November.

Recreation and culture prices rose by 0.5% in the month to October 2026, compared with a rise of 0.1% a year ago. This led to a 12-month rate of 2.7% in October 2026, up from 2.3% in September.

There were small upward contributions from action cameras, laptops, DVDs bought online, water sports equipment, cat food, computer software, non-fiction paperbacks, and package holidays. There were downward contributions from DVDs purchased in-store, Blu-rays bought online, CD albums, boats, computer games bought online, and live music.

Prices in the restaurants and hotels division rose by 3.4% in the 12 months to October 2026, down from 3.8% in the 12 months to September 2026. On a monthly basis, prices fell by 0.4% in October 2026, compared with being little changed a year ago.

The downward contribution mainly came from restaurants and cafes where prices rose by 0.3% compared with a rise of 0.6% a year ago. There was a smaller downward contribution from hotels where prices fell by 3.8% compared with a fall of 3.4% a year ago.
